source.title: When Does Few-Shot Prompting Help? A Systematic Empirical Study of Shot-Count Effects Across Model Scale, Architecture, and Output Parsing Robustness

page_placements.theme: Evaluation protocols change measured scaling and rankings
Context length and prompting have their own conditional scaling curves

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: It compares downstream classification performance across models of different stated sizes, but does not use the original pretraining-loss or training-compute measurements. This bears on V6 only; the models are not a controlled scale sweep.
record.gate_note: The study measures prompted AG News classification F1 across models and shot counts, not held-out pretraining loss, training tokens, training compute, or compute-optimal allocations. It does not test power-law fits, extrapolation, fixed-parameter architecture effects, or the fit choices in V7. Scaling laws are cited as context. The F1 results across models bear on V6; parser comparisons are recorded separately as measurement findings, not as evidence about scaling laws.
record.test_reason: The study measures how shot count changes AG News classification F1 for five prompted LLMs, plus a parser artifact. It does not vary scale in a controlled way. The models differ in family, generation, architecture (dense vs MoE) and tuning, and two have no stated size. Scaling laws (Kaplan, Hoffmann) are cited only as background. The authors' scale remark, that a 70B model 'benefits less from few-shot examples than an 8B model', concerns shot-count benefit, not whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. So it is a related but different construct, not a test of V6 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude there is no universal optimal shot count. They describe four behavioural regimes: calibrated (Gemini, GPT-4o-mini), format-dependent (Llama 3.1 8B), zero-shot specialist (Llama 4 Scout), and U-shaped (Llama 3.3 70B, every nonzero shot count significantly below zero-shot). They say the optimal k is not predictable from scale alone. They also report a parsing artifact that deflated Llama 3.3 70B F1 by up to 206%, and recommend reporting parse failure rate alongside F1. They do not evaluate scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: No reproduction or application of the original scaling-law training and fitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: Shot count changes classification F1 substantially and differently by model. The parser choice changes Llama 3.3 70B's measured parse failures and F1.

fits_no_version.finding: Few-shot benefit is not monotonic in model size. Llama 3.1 8B gains +0.34 F1 from 0 to 2 shots, while Llama 3.3 70B loses 0.27 at 2 shots and stays below its zero-shot score at every nonzero shot count (p<0.0001). The optimal shot count ranges from 0 to 8 across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sensitivity of prompted classification to the number of in-context demonstrations is model-specific and is not predicted by parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: For Llama 3.3 70B, the original substring parser failed on 19.5–76% of outputs, depending on shot count. Its measured F1 (0.256–0.796) was far below the corrected-parser F1 (0.635–0.907), and the gap grew with shot count up to k=5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-parser robustness can materially change measured downstream task performance of LLMs, and the bias can depend on prompt configuration.

record.problems: One dataset and task, n=200, and one fixed demonstration selection; model families and sizes are not a controlled scale sweep. The paper notes that the sample size is insufficient to detect some small F1 differences. Selected confidence intervals are reported, not for every configuration.
record.rows_left_out: None. Table 5 permutation-test comparisons are not separate outcome rows because the corresponding F1 results are already recorded in r01–r30.

untested.parts: No pretraining-loss measurements or parameter/token/compute sweeps.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No controlled scale series and no relation to pretraining loss. Model sizes are partly unknown and confounded with family, generation and architecture.
No fitted exponents or fit-choice analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2/V6 limits_scope' is withdrawn. V6 would need performance tracked against scale or pretraining loss in a comparable model series. Here five heterogeneous commercial and open models of mostly unknown or confounded size are evaluated on one task (n=200) for shot-count effects. The only scale-related argument concerns few-shot benefit, a different construct, and is recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No pretraining-loss measurements or sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run scaling-law fits or larger-run extrapolation.
No fixed-compute allocation experiments or parameter/token growth trends.
No comparison of architectures at fixed parameter count.
Only text classification with prompting is studied; no cross-modality or training-regime scaling-law tests.

Tests classification performance for one task across differently sized and architecturally different models, but not performance as a function of pretraining loss, nor a controlled or broad downstream-task scale trend.
No fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal fits, or tests of how such fits depend on setup.

relation.reason: The introduction cites scaling laws and Section 7.3 contrasts few-shot benefit with scaling intuitions, but the study neither tests the listed scaling-law versions nor applies a scaling law as a tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments vary demonstration count for frozen models and compare output parsers. They do not test a scaling-law version: model size is confounded with generation, architecture and tuning, and no loss-scaling fit or downstream scaling prediction is evaluated.

source_check.notes: All listed values and confidence intervals match the tables; the two-shot changes are +0.3414 and -0.2715. The parser failure explanation is internally inconsistent: Listing 1 would match World inside the example that Section 5.3 says it cannot parse.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The tested AG News task, models, and shot counts
reader_labels.reason: F1 varies substantially with shot count and across different model families/sizes, so these results do not establish a general downstream-performance trend predictable from scale; see r01–r30. The comparison is not a controlled scaling sweep.
